abstract:
Researchers studying how gut microbes modify bile acids have identified changes in the metabolic activity of the gut microbiome associated with exceptional longevity in humans, and found that amplifying the same activity with engineered bacteria improved metabolic health in aged mice.

The post Gut Microbome and Bile Acid Modification Linked with Longevity appeared first on GEN - Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News.

metadata.author: Sophia Ktori

content.value:
Researchers from the University of California San Diego have identified changes in the metabolic activity of the gut microbiome associated with exceptional longevity in humans, and found that amplifying the same activity with engineered bacteria improved metabolic health in aged mice.

“Many studies of aging focus on what goes wrong as we get older, but our findings suggest that some changes in the gut microbiome may actually represent the body’s attempt to preserve metabolic health,” said Amir Zarrinpar, MD, PhD, Stuart and Barbara L. Brody Endowed Chair in Circadian Biology and Medicine, and professor of medicine at UC San Diego School of Medicine. “If we can identify those beneficial functions and safely strengthen them, we may eventually be able to develop new ways to promote healthier aging.”

Zarrinpar is senior and corresponding author of the researchers’ published paper in Cell Metabolism, titled “Microbial bile acid deconjugation counters metabolic decline in aging.”

For their reported study the researchers focused on how gut microbes modify bile acids. Gut bacteria produce enzymes called bile salt hydrolases (BSH) that chemically modify bile acids, allowing them to influence pathways involved in metabolism, inflammation and the body’s internal clock. “Gut microbes modify bile acids through several reactions, including deconjugation by bile salt hydrolase (BSH),” the team wrote. “Deconjugated bile acids can regulate host gene expression and signaling pathways, including those involved in metabolism, inflammation, and circadian rhythms.”

The gut microbiome—the community of bacteria and other microbes living in the digestive tract—changes throughout life and plays an important role in metabolism, inflammation, and other aspects of health. Previous research has linked age-related changes in the microbiome with frailty, chronic inflammation, and disease, while other studies have found distinctive microbiome features among people who age exceptionally well.

The researchers first studied young and aged mice and found that aging was associated with increased microbial activity related to BSH and greater bile acid modification. To determine whether a similar pattern occurred in humans, they reanalyzed publicly available data from a human aging cohort. The analysis included bile acid measurements from 48 young adults, 107 older adults, and 125 centenarians. The centenarian group showed higher ratios of certain modified bile acids than both younger groups.

Analysis of microbiome data also found greater abundance of a gene associated with BSH activity among centenarians compared with the older adult group. “Individuals with exceptional longevity show a similar bile acid deconjugation signature, suggesting an association with resilient or exceptional aging,” the team pointed out.

They then asked whether enhancing this microbial function could produce health benefits. The researchers engineered a strain of bacteria native to the gut to continuously produce BSH, and introduced the bacteria into 82-week-old mice—considered aged. A single treatment resulted in stable colonization, allowing the bacteria to persist and produce the enzyme over time.

Approximately 20 weeks after treatment, mice receiving the BSH-producing bacteria had significantly improved insulin sensitivity and modestly improved glucose tolerance compared with mice receiving a matched control bacterium. By 32 weeks, the treated mice also showed changes consistent with lower body weight and fat mass and greater lean mass. Other findings pointed to increased use of fat for energy, improved mitochondrial function, and changes in gene activity related to inflammation and the body’s internal clock. “Using engineered native bacteria, we further increased luminal BSH activity in aged mice and improved insulin sensitivity, accompanied by supportive changes in body composition and other metabolic readouts,” the investigators commented.

The results do not show that the microbial changes caused exceptional longevity in humans or that the engineered bacteria can extend lifespan. The authors note that centenarians and aged mice are not directly comparable, and the human findings provide supporting rather than definitive evidence. “We also acknowledge that aged mice and individuals with exceptional longevity are not directly equivalent and therefore consider the centenarian data corroborative rather than definitive evidence,” they stated. “From this perspective, increased BSH activity may serve as a marker of, or potential contributor to, metabolic resilience during aging. More studies in people will be needed to determine whether increased BSH activity is a marker of healthy aging, a contributor to it, or both.”

The study also points toward a broader possibility: rather than attempting to replace the entire gut microbiome, researchers may eventually be able to identify beneficial microbial functions and selectively enhance them. In their paper they noted, “Together, these findings suggest that elevated BSH activity may have a protective role during aging. They challenge the view that age-related changes in bile acid biotransformations are uniformly detrimental, highlighting microbial bile acid modulation as a potential strategy to improve late-life metabolic health.”

Future studies will investigate how different forms of BSH affect bile acid metabolism, inflammation, energy use, and other aspects of aging, as well as whether the approach works similarly in females, given established differences in aging based on sex.

“The goal isn’t simply to live longer—it’s to understand the biology that allows some people to remain resilient as they age,” said Zarrinpar. “The microbiome gives us an intriguing opportunity because, unlike many aspects of aging, it may be something we can modify. This study gives us a starting point for asking whether beneficial microbial functions can be amplified to help preserve metabolic health later in life.”
